title: Sherpa Tensing — Descent Twelve: Future Perfect Passive (C1)
description: Four words of auxiliary and not a person in sight. Stand at a point in the future, look back, and this says the thing is already behind you — without…

hero.lede: Four words of auxiliary and not a person in sight. Stand at a point in the future, look back, and this says the thing is already behind you — without committing anybody to having done it. Contracts are full of it, and that is not an accident.

sections.label: Descent briefing
sections.title: When to use it
sections.lead: The passive is not a different tense. It is the future perfect with the doer let go — and the reason you let them go is always one of these six.

cards.head: You do not know who
cards.body: Nobody can tell you the doer, so the sentence does without one.
cards.ex: "The road will have been resurfaced by then."

cards.head: The doer does not matter
cards.body: The event is the news; who did it is a footnote.
cards.ex: "All the units will have been sold before completion."

cards.head: The doer is obvious
cards.body: Saying it would be a waste of everyone's time.

cards.head: You would rather not say
cards.body: The passive is how English removes a person from a sentence.
cards.ex: "The matter will have been resolved by Friday."

cards.head: Putting the important thing first
cards.body: Whatever you put at the front is what the sentence is about.
cards.ex: "Every invoice will have been settled by the year end."

cards.head: Putting the doer back with by
cards.body: When the doer is the point, it goes at the end.
cards.ex: "The site will have been cleared by the contractor."

cards.head: Negative
cards.body: the not goes after the first auxiliary
cards.ex: "The forms won't have been processed by Monday."

cards.head: Questions
cards.body: the first auxiliary moves to the front

cards.head: With the doer
cards.ex: "It will have been cleared by the contractor."

charts.head: Turning an active sentence around
charts.note: Three moves, always the same: the object comes to the front, the verb becomes will have been + participle, and the old subject either disappears or goes to the back behind by. Only the middle step changes from camp to camp.

head: Active
Passive
What moved
rows: They will have resurfaced the road.
The road will have been resurfaced.
The contractor will have cleared the site.
The site will have been cleared by the contractor.
The contractor stayed, at the end.
They will have sold all the units.
All the units will have been sold.

charts.head: Conjugation chart
charts.note: Four fixed words and then the participle. Nothing changes for the subject at all — this is the longest form on the mountain and the least trouble to conjugate.

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Almost every error with this one is one of these three.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: It will have been finish by six.
It will have been finished by six.
After been comes the participle. Four auxiliaries do not change that.
After will the verb is always the plain form: have, never has.
By Friday it will be resolved.
By Friday it will have been resolved.
A deadline needs the perfect. Will be resolved says when, not already done.

charts.note: Neither is better. The question is only what the sentence is about — because whatever you put at the front is what the reader will think it is about.

head: Question
Passive
Active
rows:
The thing it happens to.
"The road will have been resurfaced."

The one who does it.
"They will have resurfaced the road."
Often not — and you do not need to.
Yes, and you are naming them.
At the end with by, or nowhere at all.
At the front, as the subject.
Longer by two or three words.
Usually shorter. Prefer it when both work.

charts.example: Read a completion clause in any contract and you will find this form doing quiet work: the works will have been completed to the satisfaction of the surveyor. Deadline met, standard stated, and nobody named as the one who has to meet it. That is the sentence to learn to notice.

sections.label: Trail markers
sections.title: Signal words

signals.head: Verbs with no passive at all

sections.example: The test for whether a verb can go passive: does it take an object? They built it has one, so it turns. It happened has none, so it cannot.

sections.label: Interactive
sections.title: The event, and the doer you dropped

diagram.intro: The block is the same block as the ascent, lit from above instead of fading into the dark — because the tense has not changed, only the light. Inside it sits a dashed box: the doer. It is drawn inside the event rather than beside it because the doer is not a moment in time, it is a part of the sentence — and it is dashed because most of the time nobody says it. Click either to see it in a sentence.

panels.head: The doer — optional, and usually gone
items: … by the year end, and by nobody in particular.

quiz.explain: By then is a deadline, so the perfect: will have been + participle.
Will have been is the same for every subject. Sell / sold / sold.
Will have been notified — with, as ever, nobody doing the notifying.
Will have been cleared, with the doer behind by.

quiz.prompt: I _____ at five, so ring after that. (finish)
quiz.explain: At five names when the action happens, so camp seven, and I am the one doing it.
After been comes the participle, however many auxiliaries are stacked in front.
By Friday is a deadline, so the future perfect passive.

quiz.prompt: Every invoice _____ by the year end. (settle)
quiz.explain: Will have been settled. Every invoice is singular in form.
Will have been moved says it will already have happened to us.

quiz.prompt: By the time you land, the room _____ . (prepare)
quiz.hint: By the time sets the deadline.
quiz.explain: By the time sets a deadline, so the main clause takes the future perfect passive.

quiz.prompt: By the time you _____ , the room will have been prepared. (land)
quiz.explain: The clause that sets the deadline stays in the present, even though it describes the future.

quiz.prompt: Nothing _____ before the report is read. (decide)
quiz.explain: Nothing is the subject and it decides nothing, so the passive.

results: Clean run. You can turn a sentence around and you know when the doer is worth keeping.
Solid progress. Worth a look back at the active version before you go on.
Good first attempt. The auxiliary chain is the part to read again.
